entities.name: Vestwell
entities.how_described: 本集主角：给金融机构做贴牌储蓄软件(401(k) 等)的公司，估值 20 亿美元、ARR 超 2 亿，通过摩根士丹利等渠道伙伴销售

evidence.quote: So you've built Vestwell into a pretty big company, $2 billion latest valuation. Just raised it $385 million round, over $200 million in ARR and the simplest way I can describe what you're doing is you sell software to financial institutions, to advisors that help businesses run their savings plan. Like the 401(k)s and those sort of things, where I'm sure you do a lot more. We're going to talk about all of that. But let's start at the place that really matters to us, which is the product market fit moment. You told me it took you a few years for you to feel like you found true product market fit. It was probably 2020, 2021. Take us to that time, tell us what happened then that made you feel like you're really onto something. You really kind of had the thing.
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: Yeah, sure. Our business, it's retirement, it's savings, it's college savings, disability, emergency, you know, all the tax preferred things you need for life, right? So to get your education, retirement and healthcare needs. But it's a very complicated industry. Complicated business, it's been around fifty plus years from an industry standard and, you can't just show up and have this thing that just flies off the shelf. So it takes a while to kind of entrench yourselves into some of these players and our go to market. As you mentioned, is through channel partners. So we go to market through financial institutions, we go to market through payroll HCM providers, and we go to market through government sponsored programs, out to individuals and businesses across the country. You know, we started the business, it was kind of like, let's test it with a few financial firms, advisors, RAs, and get the wheels going. But it really wasn't until about 2020, 2021, during COVID. Where we were able to ink a deal with Morgan Stanley to help be a core component of Morgan Stanley at work, and power their financial advisors and all of their businesses that they were supporting through Morgan Stanley onto the platform. That was really kind of a point in time where the market realized, oh, wow, these guys,  from a Vestwell standpoint, as well as a Morgan Stanley standpoint, are really thinking about the future of where workplace savings goes and how this becomes kind of a catalyst for the wealth savings that people are going to have over the course of their career.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: So obviously Morgan Stanley is a massive brand, but give me a sense of what that meant for Vestwell as a business. What, was that a certain committed dollar ARR? Was that commitment to introduce you to so many businesses? What did you think in your head when you're like, okay, we've signed this. This means it's going to lead to what exactly?
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: Right? I always tell people, I'm like, you have no idea how hard it was. This is a cakewalk relative to that. So yeah, so we started that business. We grew that and really what it was, was that unbundled turnkey asset management platform. A FinTech platform that we gave to financial advisors and institutions. So broker dealers, banks, RIAs, asset managers alike, and we essentially power their wealth book of business. And through that journey, you know, we were a few years into that business. Our employees wanted their own 401(k) program. So I was like, OK, I haven't really done that before. Let's go do it, so one of our sales guys had a buddy who is an advisor that sold 401(k) plans and he gave us a plan. And I was like, this is horrible. How can it be this hard, this clunky, this expensive? And that's really when the light bulb went off, like, hey, there's a problem, we're gonna go solve here. So we started with 401(k)s, you know, when it started Vestwell and now we've expanded to a whole host of different savings programs in the tax preferred lens but that was really the origination of it all.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: It's a good question and it depends on the business, ultimately. But there's a few key things. I think, ultimately, for the business, it's about recruitment and retention of the employees. And it's also about their own security, right? In the US, pension plans don't really exist anymore. There's the big question mark over social security, whether that's going to continue to hold over the course of the next few decades. This is something where you can put the control of your future in your own hands and if you can do that and not make it burdensome, right? You don't want to spend hours doing this a week. You want to spend a couple minutes maximum, right? And it really has become table stakes for employees or people that are out there interviewing saying, hey, if I'm going to come to your company and work. What are you going to give me? What are your benefit packages, right? Your health insurance, your savings programs, and all of those. And through all of this, right? When we were starting the early days of Vestwell, there was a lot of legislation that was being proposed. At the time, there was a DOL fiduciary rule that was having a big weight on how advisors could engage. There was the notion of Secure 1.0 and then Secure 2.0, and now actually they're working on Secure 3.0. Those have become some of the largest legislative tailwinds that this industry's seen since the inception of ERISA law back in the mid 70s. So it's really transformed and it's shined a light on why people need this and you see it now. Even, you know, with the current administration. Some of the things they're rolling out are on the Trump accounts and child savings, and IRA programs, and all of these different things that people are looking at. And say, we have a systemic problem. There is a crack that persists financially in this country and if we don't start to fill that crack. It is going to widen and get deeper, and we're never going to get out of it. So people are just starting to take action on it and a lot of it ultimately in this country, you know, most businesses are small and mid sized businesses. Now we do everything up and down this. We do large businesses, we have a lot of large businesses but from a volume perspective, ninety five percent of the businesses in this country would be classified as that small to midmsized business.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: When you're starting out, you're talking to donor advisors, financial advisors. What is the pitch you're giving them as to why they should pitch Vestwell to their clients?
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: Because the advisor, like, let's say I manage your wealth. You run a business, I'm like, hey, you should use Vestwell. Now I get to see the assets of everybody that you put on, all the employees.
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: Well, let me ask you one specific question about fundraising, whether it's the A, the B, the C. Size of the opportunity, this is where I see a lot of founders struggling. Some founders are way better than others at this, right? Your revenue is what it is. Your team is what it is. Your ability to take something and say, here's why this is clearly a $5 to $10 billion outcome versus here's why this is a hundred million dollar outcome. That's, it's really the story and the way you present it. How did you do it for Vestwell? I mean, on the one hand, you say, well, every business has 401(k)s. We'll sell to everybody, but then it's kind of like not believable. So I'm curious how you crafted that.
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: Yeah, so on the enterprise side and the channel partnerships, for better or worse. It was kind of all I knew, right? I had spent my career doing it, living inside of these large organizations. I started my career at Northern Trust on the ERISA side, kind of almost serendipitously, fell into this world. If you asked me back when I graduated undergrad, if I would be in the space. I would have laughed at you and it's all just taking these, weird twists and turns. And I ended up here, but I knew how to engage with large institutions, right? And think through, okay, what's your tech landscape look like? What is the business P&L owner think, right? And how to cultivate those. Now there are different sides of the house. Although I sold it to advisors in my former life and broker dealers. The wealth side operated very differently than the retirement side and I was very adamant of like, why? I was like, it all should be one. You should think about these as the same thing and Morgan Stanley, to credit James Gorman. When he was running the show over there, he was a visionary and was like, this is the future of how this business works. So you can get a like minded individual who sees the future that you also see, right? Being able to get that buy in from an executive level is a lot easier than if you're just trying to convince someone like, hey, this is where the world's going to go. So that was kind of what we did and then we got a couple of early buys. Now, I would say, well, if you looked at the first deck I built for Vestwell before we had written a line of code. There was an element of direct to consumer, right? Think of a robo advisor type thing and I remember some investors like, pick one or the other. You're not going to do both. At least you're not going to do both well. So I was like, well, I don't really know the direct to consumer side. I didn't have that performance marketing tilt to my experience. So I was like, let me go the enterprise route. Cause I know how this is going to work and at least it's way more painful. The times you get kicked in the gut or you get to the finish line and everything falls apart. I mean, it is heart wrenching oftentimes. So, you got to have some thick skin and be able to deal with that, but it's worked out well for us.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: Yeah, I would the enterprise side, right? Because I think that's closer to my core of what I gauge on. On the enterprise side, there's a lot of it. I think you have to look at some of these deals you do is, it's a long road that you're marching down and you may not make the right turn or it may not fall into your lap the first time around. But often they come around if you just continue to do it. Interesting example, this was JP Morgan. When we sold, the first time we pitched, I think it was 2018, 2019, somewhere in there. We're maybe forty people deep and all of Vestwell. And we went in there, and we pitched. We got to the finals and it was a big RFP process. And you deal with these large banks, the procurement processes. All these things are their own animals and I remember we got to the finals, everyone around the table on their side was like, we want to believe this but they're like, you guys are a Series A company or something. They're like, I don't know if we can bet on. We're JP Morgan, we're the largest bank in the world. How can we bet on this forty person startup to carry what we think is going to be the future of a lot of our business, right? So we lost that, right? And I remember the guy who ran the winning bid. I knew really well on the other side. So they're another solution. I don't want to name the name but he was selling. He called me and he goes, it was you in the finals. And I'm like, yeah. He goes, how the hell did you get there? I laughed because I've known him for decades, right? And I was like, come on, man. I was like, how long have you known me? I was like, I'm going to show up. I'm going to be there and he goes, man. He goes, if you're there now, he's like, I'm screwed. He's like, there is no way I'm going to be able to keep up with the pace at which you're moving and I was like, no, man. I'm coming for you and I'm going to get this account back. I'm like, I'm going to win JP Morgan. Sure enough, fast forward three years later. That other vendor they selected was falling apart and I got a phone call and said, hey, you guys have clearly executed and everything you told us three years ago. The markets are singing songs about you guys. Let's go through this again, right? So we did it again and we won it. And now they've become one of our largest partners, I think we run like seven or eight programs across that bank now.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: I think stay true to yourself and focus on the outcome, is really kind of the key thing. It is so easy to get caught up in noise and lose sight of where you need to go, right? And I'm just as guilty of this, right? Especially the early days, because everything's coming at you and you're just like. You're working, you know, endless hours and I think you almost have to just cancel the noise around you. Like social media, all that stuff. It's literally like doesn't exist in my life. I have my family and I have Vestwell and that is it, right? And I just focus on that because otherwise the rest of it will start to pull you in directions that are just not attitude to your life, and it's hard. And if you're passionate about it, like I am. It's a lot of fun, too, right? And you just keep grinding through it.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: So, multiple questions on this. The next one is, what is the business model with Morgan Stanley and Aegis in general?
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: Yeah, so the business model is really, we get paid off a per employer per month fee and a per saver per month fee. Typically a flat fee, something like a PEPM. Sometimes there's a basis point component depending, we're trying to over index on basis points and look like an asset manager or an advisory shop but sometimes we will do that depending on the services we're providing. So that's basically, those fees are borne by the employer and the savers on the platform. And then, Morgan Stanley really is just committing to continue to bring volume. They're not, or they're our enterprise partners. They're not necessarily going to write a check into us unless they miss the threshold of where we contractually agreed to.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: And tell me a bit more, like with Morgan Stanley or a big partner like that. What is it that they don't have that you have, that you bring to the table? Because the assumption would be like Morgan Stanley, they're going to build all this stuff. They're going to have some product like this in house, right? So what do they need you for?
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: So they typically have something in house on the wealth side. The retirement side, specifically retirement, and there's other savings programs too. It's very complex when you get to the sub accounting and the record keeping. So traditionally what firms do is they have one of two models. Model one would be they go rent a piece of software from a legacy provider, which would be like an FIS or an SS&C. They go hire a bunch of people, you know, a couple hundred people to support the business and then they hope that you have some offering that they can accrue beyond the headcount operational overhead as well as software license fees. So that's kind of, that's model number one. Model number two is you don't rent any software and you just put a bunch of providers on the shelf. So you go out there and you have, maybe a Fidelity and a Empower, you know, pick a name, right? That's out there in insurance brand, nationwide and they put a bunch of these on the shelf. And then they say, hey, if it's an advisor sold solution, here's what you're permitted to go sell, right? And they frame it or box it in some capacity. The model we took was a bit different and said, listen, why would a large global brand be putting their business with a core competitor that's really just trying to siphon that business away from that brand, be it a Morgan Stanley or whoever it is. You know, our approach was like, hey, you should have the most modern, elegant experience possible. It should be low cost and it should be yours. It shouldn't be, you know, trying to compete with someone else that you're putting on the shelf.  Because you can't operationalize it yourself. So we said, hey, listen, we'll put you in the market. It's your product, it's your brand, it's your advisors. It's, you know, your asset management if you want it and we'll do it all front to back, and you have zero overhead to do it. And that kind of really flipped the tables with how we were able to engage and got people to say, oh, I can do this myself. Yet I don't have to go hire, you know, an army of people and go rent legacy software, and try to grow a business out of it.

Which is more of a long tail, and just go deep on how you cracked that. What is the playbook that you used to get into, like we said. Either Morgan Stanley on that side or the long tail of advisors that fed your business for the first few years?

entities.name: John Hancock
entities.how_described: 本集说它是与摩根大通同样剧本的另一例：路演到终点线崩塌，后来又转回来成为最大伙伴之一

evidence.quote: Really, it was kind of like we just. I remember maybe once a quarter, just like, hey, remember this? We said we're going to do this, we did this, right? We said we're going to do this, we did this, right? Nothing grandiose or anything and then, you know, we'd go out there and we have our typical press releases, and posts, and everything we do out there, right? So it was just really just like, hey, go execute on what you said you're going to go do and the business is going to come back around. Similarly, it happened with John Hancock. We pitched John Hancock. We got to the finish line. It all fell apart and that was out of our control. That was more an internal thing. It all fell apart and then it all came back around. And now, again, they're one of our largest partners, right? It's like all these things you just kind of, as much as it was painful, and I remember just like, oh, like being so frustrated. You're like, just do what you do, guys and it's going to show up again. And we're going to win it the next time around. And that happens a lot. It's expensive and you want it the first time around. But, you know, when it shows up that second time around. There's an element of sweetness to it. You're just like, yes, we did it.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: Yes, so I have been in the financial technology world since before like FinTech, quote unquote, was a thing. Which dates me quite a bit but most relevantly, I co founded a business before this called Foliar Dynamics that got acquired by Envestnet. It used to be a public company, now it got taken private by Bain. But we were out there basically, I ran product development, I ran sales and strategy for that organization.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

It was probably 2020, 2021. Take us to that time, tell us what happened then that made you feel like you're really onto something. You really kind of had the thing.
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

Let's go do it, so one of our sales guys had a buddy who is an advisor that sold 401(k) plans and he gave us a plan. And I was like, this is horrible. How can it be this hard, this clunky, this expensive? And that's really when the light bulb went off, like, hey, there's a problem, we're gonna go solve here. So we started with 401(k)s, you know, when it started Vestwell and now we've expanded to a whole host of different savings programs in the tax preferred lens but that was really the origination of it all.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: In general, for the industry. I mean, people obviously have been setting up 401(k)s for a long time. What was the default?
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: I'm curious to understand more of the pain. Obviously, Product Market Fit, it's all about pain solution and then go to market. But the pain from the business side, like I understand that as the employee, you get connected to an advisor as part of the 401(k) or whatever. You're going through that, it's a bunch of things you don't understand. They're not that helpful, but you're like, OK, whatever. Ultimately you probably do it and it just kind of happens, right? Why does the business care so much? What is the top of that? I mean, I get it, as a business you want to provide better experience for your employees but that's not going to go to the top of your list. Necessarily, relative to all the other things you want to do. What's the thing that shines at the top of the list for a business when it comes to this?
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: Yes and also these programs, like workplace savings programs specifically. They tend to be much larger and grow much faster than an individual wealth client's assets, right? Because if you think about it, it's much easier to go sell a plan. A 401(k) plan that's going to, if let's say it starts at zero and grows past a million dollars. That's going to grow past a million dollars exponentially faster than an individual who shows up with say $100,000 and tries to grow that to a million. Because you have a base of employees underneath and you have payroll that's coming in and contributing to these programs every pay cycle, every week, every two weeks, whatever it may be. So you think about it and then you start to accrue that those assets on top of the investments. They're going to grow much larger and if for an advisor who's getting paid some element of a percentage of assets. It's a quite a lucrative business for them relative than just trying to knock on a bunch of doors to find some affluent clients.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: So it's kind of a funny story. So V1 was how do we create a, let's say, you get two or three flavors of a 401(k) solution for a micro or small business. So that would be some sort of box. It has a, you know, investment lineup that's already set up. It has all the fiduciary services and so on. And then, a business could walk and sign up, click a bunch of buttons. Think of it, I always think of it like a decision tree, right? You're just kind of like, okay, I want this option, I want this option, I want this option, I want this option. At the end of it, it's like, OK, great. Here's your document. Here's everything that's going to be submitted. There's a lot of other legal stuff that happens behind the scenes. But that was V1, right? So we went through that and people could sign up. Now, it's hard, right? You show up, it wasn't necessarily white labeled, right? When we started for everyone because we didn't really have anyone to white label for. We had a couple of clients, but they're like, who is this company? Who's his brand? Can I trust them, right? And this is a sensitive topic, right? You're asking someone for arguably the second most sensitive thing in their life outside of their family. You're saying, hey, give me your savings and let me take care of it for you. So, you know, you want to be a trusted, reliable source for that. So that was V1 that was funny. We quickly realized that we had boxed it too tight, right? That people didn't fit into those boxes all the time and they'd be like, oh, I don't really want that option. I want this option. Can you do this? And then, you start to open up the box and widen what you're doing. So we ended up sunsetting that kind of workflow. Because there were too many options that we wanted to offer. That we don't want to constrain people in that aspect. So we ended up not doing it because it got too messy. Now, fast forward last year, we rebuilt that same workflow from the ground up and it's one of our core things that flies off the shelf right now. So it was kind of like some of these early ideas that we were right with the idea. We were probably a little off with the exact structure of it. But those have kind of come full circle and now they're actually core to what we do day to day.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

evidence.quote: Your boring 401(k)s.

Your ability to take something and say, here's why this is clearly a $5 to $10 billion outcome versus here's why this is a hundred million dollar outcome. evidence.quote: And I would say I've gotten better at it, right? I definitely wasn't great when I started. I mean, if you asked me back in 2016, how big this business would be. Now, the TAM is huge, right? There's $50 trillion. At that point, I think there was a little less than $40 trillion that had been amassed and you still had half the market. Over half the market wasn't participating at all, right? So let's say today you got about $50 trillion. You got a little over half participating, right? entities.name: 贴牌纯软件 (white label software)
entities.how_described: 本集说这是 Vestwell 的核心策略：产品是你的品牌、你的顾问、你的资产管理，从头到尾全做完、伙伴零开销，翻转了与大品牌的谈判桌

evidence.quote: So this is the white label software only strategy.
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

entities.name: 企业级销售 (enterprise sales)
entities.how_described: 本集把它说成非常昂贵、销售周期长达数年、采购比手术还慢的过程；输标要按季度做触点养着，周期重复时单子会回头

evidence.quote: You know, it's something I hear often in enterprise sales and I guess the lesson is the bar is low. Most people, if they lose a sale in enterprise deals. Especially, because the little ones, they really just kind of go away. But, you know, you lose a big bid and you just kind of go to zero. You're like, OK, move on to the next one and that's it. And all it takes is a little touch point, like you said, quarterly cadence and doesn't have to be exactly that. But some sort of cadence, some sort of touch points. So you're not completely forgotten. Because the cycle is going to repeat and that's just another bad. And you do this ten twenty, thirty times over. You're going to win some of those.
evidence.speaker: Pablo Srugo

evidence.quote: Yeah, you get new leadership. Now, I've had on the flip side, too. Where you get there, you want an account, you want a deal, and then there's a riff or something, you know, the leadership gets changed. And then all of a sudden, you're like, oh, I got to start over again, right? So I think it goes both ways and, you know, enterprise sales is very expensive, right? It's some of these sales cycles that they're multiple years long. The procurement processes are, you know, slower than surgery. And, you know, but if you do it, you do it well. We spent a lot of time up front in our business knowing we're a new enterprise. On making sure our procurement, your responses were super buttoned up, right? We did our security, you know, our audits, all these things that you would typically kick the can on as a business. We pulled forward and got a lot earlier, more expensive than us but it was the right call. Because it allowed us to sail through these processes.

entities.name: PEPM
entities.how_described: 本集说商业模式是按雇主每月加按储户每月的固定费用，部分含基点成分，费用由雇主和储户承担

evidence.quote: Yeah, so the business model is really, we get paid off a per employer per month fee and a per saver per month fee. Typically a flat fee, something like a PEPM. Sometimes there's a basis point component depending, we're trying to over index on basis points and look like an asset manager or an advisory shop but sometimes we will do that depending on the services we're providing. So that's basically, those fees are borne by the employer and the savers on the platform. And then, Morgan Stanley really is just committing to continue to bring volume. They're not, or they're our enterprise partners. They're not necessarily going to write a check into us unless they miss the threshold of where we contractually agreed to.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm

entities.name: RIA
entities.how_described: 本集说创办时必须搭一个 SEC 注册的投资顾问实体，第一个客户刚上平台就被 SEC 审计，反而成了看清监管者想法的积极经历

evidence.quote: So the default was a very handheld process. Where someone would say, hey, let's talk through a whole host of options. Let's check a bunch of boxes on a planned services agreement document. Let's stand up that, you know, let's choose your investments. Let's, you know, do you want safe Harbor, elective, non elective, all of these things. They're like a foreign language to most people, right? And even me, when I was at my prior company the advisors, like, hey, do you want to do this or that? And I was like, I don't know, what should I do? And the advisor is like, I can't tell you what to do. I'm like, well, you're an advisor. Give me advice, that's the whole job, right? And he's like, well, legally, I'm not really allowed to. So then that was when I was thinking like, hey, we could actually help walk people through this on their own. Much more consumable, distilled fashion that allowed people to make conscious, educated decisions without having to be an expert. Because you don't expect someone to be an expert in that space, right? That's going too far, but it's like, OK, how do you give them the confidence and all the information they need to make those right decisions, for themselves and for their business. But do so in a really streamlined fashion that doesn't become operationally intensive. So that was a lot of what we saw, but we didn't build the core of it. We didn't build the core underlying record keeping sub accounting piece when we started the business and that was simply because, we didn't know enough and I didn't know enough. And I was like, if we go down this path, we're going to chew up millions of dollars. We're going to end up with either a half baked solution that doesn't work or we're going to end up with a solution that's so tightly boxed. It's going to be so hard to open up the aperture of who we want to actually engage over the life of this business. So we kind of slow walked it, if you will and it was painful to do that. But it also was really eye opening because we learned so much about what to do as well as what not to do. When we were going to build our own and then what we started to do over time was lift out pieces of that legacy software and just rebuild it from the inside out. And then, eventually just rip and replace and re-platform the entire thing. So that was kind of the evolution of it all. But we had to stand up an RIA, right? We had to become an SEC registered advisor. So we started that, I remember we stood up an RIA and we got audited by the SEC. I think the second we put on our first business on the platform and I was like, you got to be kidding me. We literally just started this thing and now I got to go through an SEC audit. But that was also really enlightening.
evidence.speaker: Aaron Schumm
